ABSTRACT The Australian–Indonesian monsoon (AIM) is the manifestation of seasonal rainfall change and wind reversal over northern Australia and the Maritime Continent, within a region of extreme land-sea fragmentation.
This review synthesizes what is currently known about AIM evolution and mechanisms, emphasizing the Quaternary where proxy evidence, dating control, and modeling experiments are most abundant.

The AIM occupies a unique position within the global monsoon system.

It spans the equatorial region and is organized not only by large-scale ocean and atmosphere circulations but also by an unusually complex and variable geography that exerts a strong control on surface fluxes and convection [ 1 ].

The absence of strong topographic forcing and the presence of a direct near-field ocean results in a spatially structured AIM climate [ 2 ], particularly between the equatorial Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP) and the strictly monsoonal southern Maritime Continent and northern Australia [ 3 ].

The role of shelf exposure Multi-model experiments indicate that during the LGM, mean annual precipitation decreased [ 96 ] while seasonality increased [ 82 ], without a significant shift of ITCZ position [ 7 , 82 , 95 ].

Simulations of the LGM further indicate the emergence of an equatorial mode of climate variability in the Indian Ocean, similar to the modern Pacific El Niño, as a response to exposure of the Sunda and Sahul shelves due to lower glacial sea level [ 97 ].
Moreover, attribution of shelf effects remains difficult because sea level lowstands covary with low CO 2 and large ice sheets.

The most compelling model evidence therefore comes from sensitivity experiments in which sea level (land mask and bathymetry) is altered while CO 2 , ice sheets, and orbital parameters are held fixed [ 5 , 56 ].
When nearly all models misrepresent land-sea rainfall distribution and convection in the modern climate, their shelf sensitivity may not be credible.

Underestimation of low-frequency Walker circulation variability: Proxy records reveal pronounced centennial-scale variability in the Walker circulation and its impact on AIM rainfall, particularly during the last two millennia [ 79 ].

Linear responses versus threshold behavior: Proxy evidence from equatorial IPWP sites demonstrates that deep tropical convection exhibits threshold behavior, responding strongly to Heinrich stadials but weakly or not at all to most Dansgaard–Oeschger events [ 36 , 67 ].

However, while disagreements among proxy records can reflect genuine spatial structure, apparent agreement among proxies may reflect shared sensitivity to moisture source or seasonality rather than to precipitation amount.

The next phase of progress will require routine ensembles, explicit quantification of paleogeographic uncertainty, improved simulation of Maritime Continent convection and the diurnal cycle, and proxy-aware evaluation using isotope-enabled modeling and multi-proxy approaches.
